deep.reconstruction:
Setting. The modulus is the Gaussian prime M = 5+4i, with norm 41 (the header reads '5+4i ...... 41'). Since Z[i]/(M) is isomorphic to Z/41, and from 5+4i ≡ 0 we get i ≡ -5·4^{-1} ≡ 9 (mod 41), with 9^2 = 81 ≡ -1. Every computation on the page can be checked by replacing i with 9 mod 41.

(A) Index table, middle block, rows 1-10. Gauss takes the primitive root g = 2-i (≡ -7 ≡ 34 mod 41) and lists g^n for n = 1..10 as minimal residues mod M (column 2):
2-i, -1+i, -1+3i, -2i, 3, 2+2i, 1-2i, -4, 1+3i, i.
The recursion is r_{n+1} = r_n·(2-i) reduced mod M. For example (2-i)^2 = 3-4i ≡ -1+i, and g^5 ≡ 3. Row 10 shows g^10 ≡ i, so ind(i) = 10.
- Column 1 is r·conj(M) = r·(5-4i). Examples: (2-i)(5-4i) = 6-13i and (-1+i)(5-4i) = -1+9i.
- Columns 3-4 are i times columns 1-2, which give the entries for n+10 (n = 11..20). Examples: i(6-13i) = 13+6i and i(2-i) = 1+2i, labelled 11.
- The point of column 1: x·conj(M) = 41·(x/M). This is the numerator of x/M over the common denominator 41, and its coordinates lie in [-20,20]. Two numbers are congruent mod M exactly when their products with conj(M) are congruent mod 41 coordinatewise. So the pair (Re, Im) of x·conj(M) reduced into (-20,20] serves as a lookup key for the index of x.

(B) Top three blocks. Here 1+i ≡ 10 has index 32 and order 5, since (1+i)^5 = -4-4i ≡ -40 ≡ 1. Each block lists a coset of the order-5 subgroup <1+i> (index classes 0, 3, 6 mod 8):
- Block 1 starts at 1: 1, 1+i, 2i, -2+2i, -4. Indices 0, 32, 24, 16, 8.
- Block 2 starts at 1+2i: 1+2i, -1+3i, -3i, -1+2i, -3+i. Indices 11, 3, 35, 27, 19.
- Block 3 starts at 1-i: 1-i, 2, 2+2i, 4i, -i. Indices 22, 14, 6, 38, 30.
- The left column is again x·(5-4i), e.g. (1-i)(5-4i) = 1-9i. Each step multiplies by 1+i and reduces by multiples of 41 (e.g. (7+19i)(1+i) = -12+26i ≡ -12-15i). Each cycle closes after 5 steps.

(C) Verification block, top left, 4 rows × 9 columns. Write p+qi for the column-1 entries of rows 2-10 of table (A). Gauss computes (p+qi)(5+4i) as two rows each:
- real part 5p + (-4q);
- imaginary part 5q + 4p.
Every sum is a multiple of 41, e.g. -5-36 = -41 and 45-4 = 41. This checks that (p+qi)/41·M recovers the small residue, e.g. (-1+9i)(5+4i) = -41+41i, giving -1+i. It confirms the entries are multiples of conj(M).

(D) Main application: indices of primary primes m and of conj(m) modulo M. Gauss writes m = a+2bi and computes m·conj(M) = (5a+8b) + (-4a+10b)i as four rows: 5a, 8b, -4a, 10b. He adds them and reduces mod 41 into (-20,20]. He also computes conj(m·M) = conj(m)·conj(M). He then looks the pairs up in table (A)/(B).

(D1) Small block, m = 3+2i, 1+4i, -5+2i, -1+6i, 5+4i (norms 13, 17, 29, 37, 41). Rows: 15, 5, -25, -5, 25 / 8, 16, 8, 24, 16 / -12, -4, 20, 4, -20 / 10, 20, 10, 30, 20. The resulting list (pair | index) is:
- m = 3+2i: (-18,-2) | 26; conj(m): (7,19) | 3.
- m = 1+4i: (-20,16) | 8; conj(m): (-11,17) | 19.
- m = -5+2i: (-17,-11) | 29; conj(m): (8,10) | 24.
- m = -1+6i: (19,-7) | 33; conj(m): (12,15) | 15.
- m = M: (0,0) | *; conj(M): (9,1) | 32.

(D2) Big right block, m = 7+2i, -5+6i, -3+8i, 5+8i, 9+4i, -1+10i, 3+10i, -7+8i (norms 53, 61, 73, 89, 97, 101, 109, 113).
- Pairs for m·conj(M): (2,-18), (-1,9), (17,11), (16,20), (20,-16), (-6,13), (14,-3), (-3,-14). Indices from the tables: 36, 2, 9, 38, 28, 21, 17, 7.
- Pairs for conj(m)·conj(M): (-14,3), (-8,-10), (-6,13), (-7,-19), (-12,-15), (-4,-5), (16,20), (15,-12).
- The first crossed-out row (10, 30, 40, ...) is the 10b row, entered in the wrong place and then rewritten.

(D3) Bottom left block, m = -11+4i, 7+10i, 11+6i, -13+2i, -9+10i, -7+12i (norms 137 to 193).
- Pairs for m·conj(M): (2,-18), (-7,-19), (-3,-14), (-16,-20), (-5,4), (13,6).
- Pairs for conj(m·M): (11,-17), (-5,4) [written -8?], (-10,8), (9,1), (-3,-14), (-1,9).
- '-55+44 / -14+30' is scratch for the same procedure.

All these m are primary: m ≡ 1 mod (2+2i). Since g^10 ≡ i, m^{(41-1)/4} ≡ i^{ind m}. So ind(m) mod 4 gives the biquadratic character (m/M)_4, and ind(conj m) mod 4 gives (conj m / M)_4. This is (my inference) material for testing biquadratic reciprocity or the Int/Dec lemma of the previous page. The next page continues with classes 0-3 of primary numbers and (m-1)/(2+2i).
errors: In the bottom 2x6 table, the second entry of the third row appears as -8. For m = 7+10i, conj(m·M) = -5-78i ≡ (-5, 4) mod 41, so it should be -5. Either a slip by Gauss or an ambiguous glyph.

The verification block (C) as transcribed ('-5+55', '-36+76') fails the mod-41 check in its second column. The column must be 5·7 = 35 and -4·19 = -76 (p+qi = 7+19i). This is likely a misreading, or else a sign slip.
No other errors found. Every index, product and reduction I checked (about 60 entries) is correct.

results.what: Primitive root 2-i modulo the Gaussian prime 5+4i (norm 41), with an index table of minimal residues; g^10 ≡ i, ind(1+i) = 32, ind(1+2i) = 11, ind(1-i) = 22
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones 1801 for Z/p; Gaussian-integer residues in Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum 1828/1832); index tables by Jacobi (Canon arithmeticus, 1839)

results.what: Representing a residue x mod M by x·conj(M) = 41·(x/M), so that coordinatewise reduction mod 41 into (-20,20] gives a unique lookup key for the residue class
results.modern_name: Isomorphism Z[i]/(π) ≅ Z/p combined with the lattice conj(π)Z[i]; reduction of x/π to a fundamental domain

results.what: Cosets of the order-5 subgroup generated by 1+i mod 5+4i
results.modern_name: Coset decomposition of (Z[i]/π)^* by a subgroup (cyclotomic classes)

results.what: Indices mod 5+4i of primary primes m and conj(m) of norm up to 193, giving the quartic characters (m/M)_4 = i^{ind m}
results.modern_name: Numerical computation of biquadratic (quartic) residue symbols, data for quartic reciprocity
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (biquadratic reciprocity stated 1832; proofs published by Jacobi/Eisenstein 1844)

deep.surprise_reason: These are computational tables of indices and quartic characters modulo a Gaussian prime, in the context of Gauss's well-documented biquadratic residue work. The lookup trick via x·conj(M) mod 41 is neat but is a computational convenience. No new theorem appears.
